The FOMC’s move on March 15, 2020 to cut the federal funds rate to the effective lower bound and launch large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS is aligned with the literature on policy at the zero lower bound and the credit channel. At the ZLB, balance-sheet policies and forward guidance can support aggregate demand (Eggertsson; Rudebusch and Svensson, 1997), while stabilizing credit spreads and firm balance sheets mitigates the financial accelerator (Bernanke, Gertler, and Gilchrist, 1996). Falling market-based inflation compensation and below-target inflation increase disinflation and debt-deflation risks, making aggressive easing consistent with Taylor-rule and optimal-rule perspectives (Romer and Romer; Taylor rule; Rudebusch and Svensson, 1997). In parallel, expanded repo operations and dollar swap lines address global dollar funding stress, consistent with the “liquidity value of money” framework from Keynes–Hicks and subsequent models (Eggertsson; Rudebusch and Wu, 2007), and LSAPs help compress term premia. Nevertheless, because the pandemic imposes both demand and supply disruptions, the literature indicates monetary policy cannot fully offset near-term output losses (Eichenbaum and Evans; Ramey), so the near-term outlook remains negative even as these tools meaningfully cushion the downturn.
